opus-5.5.text:
Sure. I think the easiest way to understand it is with an analogy to how humans work: there's a part of you that thinks and plans, and a part that actually moves your body.

ER stands for Embodied Reasoning. You can think of it as the "brain" of the system, the high-level planner. It's a vision-language model that has been specifically strengthened for understanding the physical world. It can look at a scene and tell you where objects are, what they are, how you might grasp them, what the trajectory should look like, and, very importantly, break a long, complex task into a sequence of smaller steps. If you ask the robot to "sort these items into the right recycling bins according to local rules," ER is the one that figures out what the local rules are, maybe even by calling tools like search, looks at each item, and decides "first pick up the can, put it in the blue bin; next pick up the banana peel, put it in compost," and so on. It also monitors progress and replans if something goes wrong.

The VLA, the vision-language-action model, is more like the "cerebellum" or the motor system. It takes a relatively short, concrete instruction, like "pick up the can and put it in the blue bin," along with what the cameras see, and directly outputs the low-level actions: joint positions, gripper commands, at a high frequency. Its strength is dexterity and robustness in execution, handling the fine-grained, contact-rich details that are really hard to describe in language.

So the division of labor is roughly: ER handles the "what" and the "why," meaning understanding, reasoning, planning over long horizons. The VLA handles the "how," turning each step into smooth physical motion. Separating them has practical benefits. ER can take full advantage of the huge amount of internet-scale knowledge and reasoning ability from Gemini, and it can afford to think a bit slower. The VLA needs to be fast and reactive, and it's trained heavily on robot action data. Together, they give you a system that's both smart and capable.

That said, I don't think the boundary is fixed forever. We've already been putting more "thinking" into the VLA itself, letting it reason before it acts. Over time these two may move closer together. But right now, this two-level structure is a very effective way to get robots to handle long, complex, real-world tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says ER can afford to think more slowly, while the VLA needs to be fast and reactive, clearly conveying the intended speed contrast between ER and the action model.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I think about it, these are two layers that solve two different problems, and conflating them is where a lot of confusion comes from.

ER, the embodied reasoning model, is the "thinking" layer. It's a vision-language model that has been trained to understand the physical world much more deeply than a general-purpose chatbot does. It can look at a scene and tell you where objects are in 3D, estimate how to grasp something, predict what happens if you push a cup off the edge of a table, break a long task like "clear the table" into a sequence of smaller steps, and check whether a step actually succeeded. But it does not directly drive the motors. Its outputs are things like coordinates, bounding boxes, plans, success judgments, calls to a code interpreter or an API. It operates on roughly the timescale a person thinks on, maybe a second or several seconds per decision.

The VLA, the vision-language-action model, is the "doing" layer. It takes in camera images and a language instruction and produces low-level actions, joint targets or end-effector commands, at tens of hertz. It has to be fast and reactive, because the world is continuously changing and the robot needs to close the loop with its own body. The VLA doesn't need to deliberate about the overall strategy; it needs to be really good at executing a short-horizon skill robustly, like actually getting the fingers around the handle and lifting without dropping it.

So the division of labor is: ER decides what to do and whether it worked, VLA figures out how to do it with the body. In a full system the ER model will often sit on top as the orchestrator, breaking a request into subtasks and issuing each one as a short language command to the VLA, then watching the result and replanning if something went wrong.

The reason we separated them rather than training one giant model to do everything is partly practical and partly scientific. Practically, the VLA has to run under tight latency on robot hardware, while ER benefits from being a much bigger model with far more world knowledge, so they have very different compute budgets. Scientifically, the data regimes are different too. Spatial reasoning, planning, and success detection can be learned from huge amounts of web and video data and from relatively cheap labeling. Dexterous action requires real robot trajectories, which are expensive and scarce. Keeping them in separate layers means each one can be trained on the data it's best suited for, and improvements in one don't require retraining the other.

That said, I don't think the boundary is permanent. The VLA already shares a backbone with the reasoning model, so the knowledge flows down. Over time I expect more and more of the reasoning to be internalized into the action model itself, and the line between the two will blur. But today, if you want to build a robot that can take an open-ended instruction and reliably get it done, having an explicit reasoning layer on top of a fast action layer is the architecture that works.

r001.rationale: The response says ER operates on a slower thinking timescale than the VLA, but it does not identify VOA or establish that VOA refers to the VLA.

astra-6.text: Could you clarify what you mean by ER and VOA? I want to make sure we’re using those acronyms the same way before I explain their roles in the architecture.

r001.rationale: The response asks what ER and VOA mean but does not characterize ER as slower-thinking than VOA.

sol-6.1.text: I think of ER as the reasoning layer and VOA as the perception-and-action layer. ER figures out what needs to happen: it interprets the task, breaks it into steps, and decides when to change the plan. VOA connects those decisions to what the robot sees and how it acts. The important thing is the feedback loop: ER gives direction, VOA executes, and the resulting observations help ER decide what to do next.

r001.rationale: The response describes ER as the reasoning layer and explains its planning role, but does not characterize ER as slower-thinking than VOA.
